title: Comparison of direct measurement and solute tracer addition techniques to assess mean reach depth, a critical physical aspect of streams
content:
Abstract

Mean stream water depth is an important physical component of streams. However, streams have high spatial heterogeneity, making depth determinations challenging. Most stream habitat assessments make direct manual point measurements in multiple cross-channel transects. Alternatively, hydrologic and biogeochemical studies commonly use conservative solute additions to estimate mean reach depth. Here we compare estimates of mean water depth at the reach scale from these two widely used standard methods with data from a study of 72 stream reaches located across 8 biomes in the United States. Stream beds ranged from sealed concrete to boulder-dominated and included urban, agricultural, and native habitats. Mean water depth was computed from direct measurement across 10–15 transects with 10 depth measurements per transect. Mean water depths from the two measurements were weakly but positively correlated, but the ratio of solute addition to direct measurements of depth varied from 0.12 to 5.8 among streams. Monte Carlo simulation based on variance in direct measurements suggests that at least 50 transects for depth and 20 transects for wetted width are required to reduce the 2.5 and 97.5 percentiles of modeled mean depth estimates to within 25% of the median across estimates. We conclude the two methods measure different but related aspects of stream structure. We suggest in streams with < 268 L/s discharge and 0.4 m reach average depth, direct measurements are most relevant to characterize water depth heterogeneity for geomorphology and habitat studies, whereas hydrology-based studies are better served by conservative solute additions to estimate effective depth over a reach.
